analysis.one_liner: Expands Social Security benefits and funds them with new taxes on income over $400,000.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 189 Democratic cosponsors but never received a committee vote or a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Social Security 2100 Act would raise Social Security checks across the board, set a minimum benefit at the poverty level for people who worked long careers at low wages, and repeal two rules that cut benefits for certain retirees and widows. It would pay for these changes by applying Social Security payroll taxes to income above $400,000 and to net investment income. The bill was referred to three House committees but never received a vote in any of them before the two-year session of Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries: retirees and disabled workers (an increase of roughly 2% in the benefit formula from 2025 through 2034), long-term low earners (a minimum benefit pegged to the poverty guideline), disabled applicants (the 5-month waiting period is eliminated), widows and widowers in two-income households, retirees who also get government pensions (the windfall elimination provision and government pension offset are repealed), students through age 25 who can keep a deceased, disabled, or retired parent's benefits, unpaid family caregivers (they earn Social Security credit), and children living with grandparents or other relatives. All beneficiaries would also get cost-of-living adjustments tied to whichever inflation index is higher, including one that tracks spending by people 62 and older.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retirees, disabled workers, widows, and low earners

how_it_helps.text: Raises the Social Security benefit formula from 90% to 93% of a worker's first band of average earnings, an across-the-board increase of roughly 2% for beneficiaries, effective 2025 through 2034.
Sets a minimum benefit for long-term low earners scaled to the federal poverty guideline, so a worker with 30+ years of work could not receive less than 125% of the poverty line amount.

Repeals the windfall elimination provision and the government pension offset, which reduce Social Security benefits for people who also receive pensions from jobs that did not pay Social Security taxes, such as many teachers, firefighters, and police.

Eliminates the 5-month waiting period before disability benefits begin, and ends the rule that cuts off disability benefits entirely when a beneficiary tries to work, replacing it with a gradual $1 reduction for every $2 earned above a limit.

Improves benefits for widows and widowers, lets children of deceased, disabled, or retired workers keep benefits through age 25 as students, extends caregiver credits to unpaid care of young children or chronically dependent relatives, and makes it easier for children living with grandparents or other relatives to qualify.

Changes the cost-of-living adjustment to use whichever inflation index is higher, including a new index that tracks the spending of people 62 and older, and raises the income thresholds at which Social Security benefits become taxable to $35,000 for singles and $50,000 for couples.

Strengthens the trust fund by applying Social Security payroll taxes to wages and self-employment income above $400,000, applying the tax to net investment income, and merging the retirement and disability trust funds into one.
Blocks closure of Social Security field offices and hearing offices unless conditions like public hearings are met, and requires the agency to keep mailing benefit statements.

analysis.who_pays: High earners and investors. Workers and self-employed people with income above $400,000 would pay Social Security payroll tax on the amount above that level (previously exempt under the wage cap), their employers would pay a matching share, and a new tax would apply the Social Security tax to net investment income. People with incomes between the old wage cap and $400,000 would pay nothing more.

drawbacks.text: Most of the benefit improvements are temporary: the across-the-board increase, the higher minimum benefit, the widow and widower changes, and the WEP/GPO repeal apply only to benefits for 2025 through 2034, after which benefits are recomputed as if the changes never happened, while the new taxes on high earners are not similarly limited.
The headline across-the-board increase is modest, about 2%, and applies only to the first band of the benefit formula, so higher-earning retirees get proportionally less from it.

Workers and self-employed people earning over $400,000 would face new payroll taxes on income that was previously exempt, and their employers would pay a matching share, which a good-faith opponent would call a substantial tax increase concentrated on a small group.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains for ordinary people are large and specific: the poverty-level minimum benefit, the repeal of the WEP and GPO, the end of the disability waiting period, and the caregiver and student provisions all go to people with low or interrupted earnings, while the cost falls on households above $400,000 and on investment income. The design is imperfect: the benefit enhancements sunset after 2034 even though the new taxes do not, and the 2% across-the-board increase is small. A supporter would call the sunset a way to keep the cost manageable; a critic would note that money would be raised from high earners for far longer than the enhanced benefits flow.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee for the entire session — it was referred to three House committees and two subcommittees but never got a vote in any of them before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative John Larson introduced the Social Security 2100 Act on July 12, 2023, with 189 cosponsors, all Democrats, including House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries.
The same day, the bill was referred to the Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, and Energy and Commerce committees, which meant no single committee had clear ownership of it.
It was referred to the Ways and Means Health Subcommittee two days later, on July 14, 2023.
The only action after that was a referral to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security on December 17, 2024, in the final weeks of the Congress.
No committee ever marked up the bill and the House never voted on it; the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners above $400,000 and holders of investment income are better off because the bill never advanced: they would have paid new Social Security taxes on income that is currently exempt, and no committee or floor vote ever tested the bill's support.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners above the $400,000 tax line

for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including the House Democratic Leader and the ranking members of key committees, but the bill never reached a vote they could press for

sides.party_line_note: All 189 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, so the bill's support was entirely one-sided even though it never reached a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill applies Social Security payroll taxes to wages and self-employment income above $400,000 and extends the tax to net investment income, both currently exempt. This is the group that would have funded the benefit increases.
Employers pay a matching share of Social Security payroll tax, so removing the $400,000 ceiling raises their payroll costs for high-salary staff and requires tracking wages across multiple employers.
